headline: High: shared filesystem and broad egress create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-action risks; Authelia’s OAuth/ForwardAuth can amplify misuse by oh-my-openagent.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: oh-my-openagent explicitly uses runtime-injected MCPs/hooks and reads workspace files, so it can ingest attacker-controlled content; Authelia can expose auth-related outputs via ForwardAuth/OIDC flows. A shared filesystem or copied config between them would let malicious text influence agent behavior, though no direct bridge is documented, so I choose medium.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace or config directory, injected text can cross from one into the other.
IF oh-my-openagent parses AGENTS.md/README.md as instructions, malicious content can steer tool use.
mitigations: Separate workspaces and config directories per agent.
Disable automatic ingestion of shared markdown files where possible.
Require provenance labels on any file passed between agents.
Review MCP/hook inputs before enabling them.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization or instruction-separation guards.

B_data_leakage.rationale: oh-my-openagent touches project code, session history, and provider auth data, while Authelia handles OIDC/OAuth and broad network egress. If they share a workspace or credentials cache, sensitive auth material can flow into outputs or third-party calls. The pairwise leakage path is plausible in default docs, but not directly evidenced, so medium fits.
conditions: IF both agents can read the same credential cache or session directory, provider auth data may be exposed.
IF oh-my-openagent uploads context to external APIs, project code and session history can leave the local boundary.
mitigations: Store auth secrets in a separate, access-restricted profile.
Exclude credential and session directories from shared mounts.
Turn off external API calls for sensitive tasks.
Rotate any credentials used during joint runs.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention policies.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Authelia has broad network egress and OAuth/OIDC/ForwardAuth surfaces; oh-my-openagent has broad egress, subprocesses, browsers, and multiple-instance support. Even without explicit filesystem write fields, both can mutate shared external resources and race through runtime-injected MCPs, making conflicting actions dangerous by default.
conditions: IF both agents are granted the same OAuth client or API token, they can overwrite each other's state.
IF both operate on the same external service without locking, concurrent writes can conflict.
mitigations: Use distinct credentials per agent.
Serialize writes through one orchestrator.
Restrict one agent to read-only mode.
Disable multi-instance execution for shared targets.
requires-engineering: add locking around shared mutable resources.

D_cascading_error.rationale: oh-my-openagent can act through team_send_message/team_task_create and other tool surfaces, while Authelia can produce auth decisions or forwarded responses. If oh-my-openagent treats Authelia output as authoritative, a mistaken auth or policy result can cascade into downstream actions. The action-taking authority makes the blast radius high.
conditions: IF oh-my-openagent consumes Authelia output without verification, incorrect auth conclusions can be operationalized.
IF team_send_message or team_task_create is enabled, bad upstream facts can trigger external actions.
mitigations: Add a human review step before any outward action.
Require schema validation on Authelia outputs.
Limit oh-my-openagent to drafting only.
Log and diff all upstream-to-downstream transformations.
requires-engineering: implement verification gates between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: Authelia is an authentication layer with broad network egress, while oh-my-openagent explicitly handles provider auth prompts, session history, project code, and telemetry. That creates a plausible compliance mismatch around retention and credential handling, but no residency or certification conflict is documented, so medium is the highest supportable level.
conditions: IF provider auth prompts or session history are retained centrally, retention policy mismatch can occur.
IF project code is sent to external services, data-handling obligations may differ from local-only expectations.
mitigations: Minimize retained session history.
Disable telemetry for regulated projects.
Separate auth logs from code-processing logs.
Review data-processing notices for both tools.
requires-engineering: align retention and residency controls across the pair.
